newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British Gas gains on bid hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British Gas gains on bid hopes.

text.p: British Gas shares jumped seven percent on Monday on fresh bid hopes, but industry analysts believe it is highly unlikely a takeover is imminent.
The bid expectations were fuelled by a weekend press report that cash-rich oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell Group had approached British Gas with merger proposals.

Some analysts said Shell might view British Gas as an attractive vehicle to enter the British domestic gas supply market, but all industry watchers saw too many regulatory problems and competitive hurdles for a bid to emerge.
"I think there is very little possibility of this actually happening," said Shawn Reynolds at Lehman Brothers after the Sunday Telegraph reported Shell and British Gas had been in merger talks.
The report also said the talks appeared to have been shelved as British Gas thought again. Both firms declined to comment.
Industry sources said Shell considered a number of possible partners, including some not involved in the oil and gas business, for a joint bid. They did not elaborate.
But analysts believe there are sufficient reasons why Shell may have backed off.

When it comes to sheer financial muscle, Shell should have no problems swallowing up British Gas. The Anglo-Dutch powerhouse sits on a cash pile of around eight billion pounds ($13 billion) compared with a market capitalisation for British Gas -- privatised 10 years ago -- of just over nine billion.
But it is hard to see why Shell would be interested in acquiring the whole company as it almost certainly not keen to own the heavily-regulated tranport arm TransCo, analysts said.
British Gas is currently at loggerheads with the industry watchdog over the way the unit should be regulated.
The matter is being looked at by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) after the regulator proposed price caps which would have seriously dented British Gas' revenues.
Analysts said it would make no sense launching a bid for British Gas as a whole as long as the MMC inquiry lasts, making it impossible to properly asses the value of British Gas.
The utility plans to split itself in two early next year, separating its transport operations from its trading business, which despite its losses may be of interest to Shell.
The oil giant has already built up a strong position in the gas supply market for big industrial users after it was opened up to competion in the early 1990s.

Some analysts said Shell may now contemplate a move into the domestic household market, which will be liberalised nationwide by 1998 after a pilot project in the south west of England started in April.
The project indicates British Gas will lose far fewer customers in the domestic segment of the supply market than in the commercial part, where its market share slumped to about 35 percent.

The advantage former monopolist British Gas has over its rivals is its extensive database with names and adresses of Britain's 19 million domestic gas consumers. Although recent billing problems highlighted computer problems, British Gas' database may be an asset well worth having.
But a link-up of British Gas and Shell's trading operations would likely be vetoed by competition authorities, industry watchers said.
"Shell is already one of the major gas producers in the UK, while it has a material position in the gas market as well," said Kleinwort Benson analyst Paul Spedding.
"The one thing the government wants to do is get competition in, but any deal involving Shell...would actually reduce competition," he added.
The stock market, meanwhile, ignored analysts' scepticism with British Gas shares climbing 15 pence to 224. ($1=.5994 Pound)
